checkpoints: Root cause: the federated credential's `subject` is declared only for `refs/heads/main`, but the workflow run on `feature/payment-fix` produces an OIDC token whose `sub` claim is `repo:starci-academy/payment-service:ref:refs/heads/feature/payment-fix` — a completely different string that fails to match.

Azure's federated-credential subject matching is exact equality only, with no wildcard/pattern support — unlike AWS, which can use a `StringLike` condition to match many branches with a single trust policy.

Because Azure has no pattern mechanism, every branch/PR/environment that needs token exchange requires its own `azurerm_federated_identity_credential` declaring its exact subject (up to 20 credentials per identity).

This is what makes the failure hard to debug: Entra ID does not return a clear "subject mismatch" error when the subject doesn't match — the token exchange fails silently, so the job only sees a generic "login failed" message from `azure/login`, which easily misleads debugging toward the wrong direction (suspecting a missing role assignment or a wrong client-id/tenant-id) instead of the real exact-subject-string mismatch.

Fix: add a new `azurerm_federated_identity_credential` with `subject = "repo:starci-academy/payment-service:ref:refs/heads/feature/payment-fix"` (or design credentials by the pattern actually needed — one per long-lived branch, or use the `pull_request` claim for per-PR runs).
After adding the credential, re-run the pipeline to confirm the `azure/login` step now succeeds.

Prevention: add a step that decodes the real `sub` claim from the GitHub Actions OIDC token (printed in CI logs) so it can be compared directly against the declared `subject`, instead of guessing character by character next time.

Assign the policy definition at a single Management Group scope covering all relevant subscriptions, not per-subscription — a management-group-level assignment inherits down to every subscription and resource group beneath it, avoiding the tedious, error-prone task of assigning it individually across dozens of subscriptions.

The policy effect must be `deny`, not `audit` — `audit` only records the violation in a compliance report and blocks nothing, which fails to satisfy the manager's requirement to block untagged RG creation outright.

To address the manager's concern about breaking CI pipelines, first assign the policy with `enforcementMode = DoNotEnforce` (enforce = false) instead of the default `enforce = true` — in this mode the `deny` effect is evaluated but not enforced, so violating (untagged) RGs are still created normally and only flagged non-compliant in the report.
During the DoNotEnforce phase, monitor the compliance report over time to identify exactly which team or pipeline is creating violating (untagged) RGs.
Proactively notify the identified team(s) so they have time to fix their script/pipeline (add the tag) before enforcement is turned on.

Only after most violations have been cleaned up should the assignment be switched to `enforce = true`, so the `deny` effect officially takes hold — actual blocking then surprises far fewer people since everyone was already warned during the DoNotEnforce phase.

Clarify to the manager that even with `deny` enabled, untagged resource groups that existed before the assignment continue running unaffected — `deny` only blocks new create/update requests and does not automatically delete anything.
Cleaning up pre-existing untagged RGs requires a separate remediation pass, done manually or via effects like `modify`/`deployIfNotExists`.
This isn't a bug — RBAC and Azure Policy are two separate mechanisms working together, not one substituting for the other.

RBAC answers "who can perform what action at what scope" — it's the granting layer; the Owner role at subscription scope grants the senior engineer permission to create/edit/delete nearly every resource, including a storage account.
Azure Policy answers a different question — "what state a resource is allowed to exist in" — it's the guardrail layer, independent of who performs the action.

A create request only succeeds when both axes pass: RBAC must allow the action and the resulting state must not violate any applicable policy; failing either one blocks the request no matter how strong the other is.
Policy is enforced at the control plane, with ARM evaluating it before the resource is actually written — a proactive block on the write itself, not an after-the-fact audit.

Policy applies uniformly to every principal sending the request, with no exception based on RBAC role or permission level — it only cares whether the resulting state violates the rule, which is exactly why Owner isn't exempt.

This is why Policy is called Azure's real permission boundary, stronger than RBAC: if Owner were exempt, organizational guardrails would be meaningless precisely for the highest-privileged group most likely to create risky resources, whether accidentally or through compromise — making this deliberate design, not a limitation.

Colleague's "enable both to be safe" premise misunderstands the model — it's not two safety nets stacking, but an ambiguous, hard-to-audit state: answering "does object_id X have permission, and why" requires checking both the access policy AND role assignments instead of one single source.

The vault has `enable_rbac_authorization = true` (the RBAC model — data-plane permissions like get/set secret are decided by role assignments in the shared Azure RBAC system) while still declaring an `access_policy` block (the OLD model, managed locally inside the vault) — two entirely separate authorization mechanisms coexisting in the same resource.
The two models are mutually exclusive on the same vault: the azurerm provider will warn or error because it's unclear which mechanism is the source of truth for authorization.

Fix part 1: pick ONE model — for a newly-built vault (not migrating from a legacy system with existing policies), keep `enable_rbac_authorization = true` and remove the `access_policy` block entirely.

Fix part 2: replace the removed block with an `azurerm_role_assignment` resource granting the exact built-in role needed (e.g. Key Vault Secrets Officer for get/list/set, Key Vault Secrets User for read-only) to the specific object_id, scoped to this vault.

Azure recommends RBAC for new systems because it's managed centrally in the shared Azure RBAC system and auditable via Activity Log alongside every other org permission — unlike access policy, which is a separate list only queryable inside that specific vault.
Verify: re-run `terraform plan`/`apply` to confirm there are no more conflict warnings between the two mechanisms.
Verify: actually test get/set secret operations using the exact principal that was just granted the role, to confirm permissions work as expected.
Diagnose that this is a double mistake — both the SCOPE axis and the ROLE axis are wrong, and both need fixing.
Scope axis: lower the role assignment scope from the entire subscription down to the exact Resource Group owned by the billing team, immediately reducing blast radius if the identity is compromised.

Role axis: replace the broad `Contributor` role with narrow roles matched to exactly the three actual needs of the pipeline, instead of one role that allows creating/editing/deleting nearly any resource type.
Assign `Storage Blob Data Contributor` at the scope of the specific storage account itself (not the whole Resource Group) to grant blob read/write.
Assign `Key Vault Secrets User` (read-only) at the scope of the specific Key Vault itself — not the Secrets Officer role — since the pipeline never creates new secrets.

For Function App deployment, use the built-in `Website Contributor` role if it's narrow enough; otherwise define a custom `azurerm_role_definition` listing only the exact ARM actions needed (e.g. `Microsoft.Web/sites/write`, `Microsoft.Web/sites/config/write`) with `assignable_scopes` restricted to the billing team's Resource Group.

Name `azurerm_role_assignment` as the Terraform resource used to grant every role, with its `scope` pointing at the specific resource (storage account / Key Vault / Function App) — directly answering the prompt's explicit ask for which Terraform resources to use.

Justify the trade-off: many narrow permissions each matched to actual need are safer than one broad permission at a high scope, because every role assignment self-documents its own reason for existing.

Key Vault resource created with `enable_rbac_authorization = true` (RBAC authorization model), referencing the existing `azurerm_resource_group.lab` and using `data.azurerm_client_config.current.tenant_id`.
Role assignment resource grants the `Key Vault Secrets Officer` role to the current principal (`data.azurerm_client_config.current.object_id`) with `scope = azurerm_key_vault.lab.id`.
Secret resource named `db-password` is created via `azurerm_key_vault_secret`, pointing at `key_vault_id = azurerm_key_vault.lab.id`.

Order matters because with RBAC enabled, creating the vault does not itself grant data-plane permission to read/write secrets — that permission comes only from the role assignment once it has taken effect; without it (or before it propagates), the secret creation gets a `403 Forbidden`, even if the principal is Owner at the subscription level, because control-plane and data-plane permissions are separate.

Terraform infers ordering from implicit references: both the role assignment and the secret reference `azurerm_key_vault.lab` (via `.id`), so both are guaranteed to wait until the vault exists — but there is no direct reference between the role assignment and the secret resources, so Terraform cannot infer that the role assignment must finish first, and could otherwise attempt to create them in parallel.
An explicit `depends_on = [azurerm_role_assignment.secrets_officer]` must be added to the secret resource to force the correct order (role assignment first, then secret).

Even with `depends_on`, RBAC role assignment can have a short propagation delay, so a transient `403` may still occur occasionally; adding a brief `time_sleep` between the two steps is a reasonable mitigation.
The `Contributor` role at the checkout Resource Group scope is correctly least-privileged — the deploy branch of the architecture is not the problem.
The actual risk lies in the `Key Vault Secrets User` role, granted at the scope of ONE Key Vault shared by multiple teams (payment, checkout, notification).
If the checkout team's workflow is compromised (e.g., via a malicious dependency / supply-chain attack), the attacker inherits that identity's exact permissions.
The attacker can then read every secret in the shared vault — including payment's and notification's — even though the compromise originated from code completely unrelated to those teams.

The root cause is a trust-boundary mismatch: the shared vault doesn't align with the team boundary, so the blast radius spreads across the whole organization instead of staying contained to the checkout team.

Redesign: split the shared Key Vault into separate per-team vaults (e.g., checkout-secrets, payment-secrets, notification-secrets), each holding only that team's own secrets, and grant each CI identity `Key Vault Secrets User` only on its own team's vault.

After the split, a compromised checkout identity can only leak checkout's own secrets — payment and notification stay isolated, since each vault is now an independent security boundary instead of a single point of failure.

General principle: a CI identity for one team should never be able to touch another team's resources or secrets just for management convenience — every trust boundary (team, dev/staging/prod environment) should get its own identity and vault, accepting more identities/vaults as a worthwhile cost for a much smaller blast radius.
An image is a set of immutable filesystem layers plus metadata (env, entrypoint, history) — it has no state and cannot run on its own, more like a static "mold" sitting on disk.
A container is a process launched from an image — the image itself never runs.
Docker gives each container its own writable layer (Copy-on-Write mechanism) on top of the image's read-only layer stack — this is the only part each container owns individually.
Every change a container makes (new file, edited file) is written to its own writable layer, never touching the image's original layers.

Docker uses a union filesystem (OverlayFS) to mount the same read-only image layers into every container, so those layers exist only once on physical disk no matter how many containers share the image — Docker never duplicates the image data per container.

The extra disk usage from running N containers off the same image is only N times the size of each container's writable layer (usually a few MB if the container doesn't write much new data), not N times the whole image size — which is exactly why disk usage grew only a few dozen MB instead of several GB.
Correctly names the root cause as Dockerfile INSTRUCTION ORDER, not `npm ci` itself getting inherently slower.
States that a Docker layer's cache key is derived from the parent layer's digest plus the instruction text (and, for COPY/ADD, a checksum of the copied files).
States that invalidating one layer invalidates every layer built on top of it (cache dependency cascades forward through the build graph).
Identifies that in the given Dockerfile `COPY . .` sits before `RUN npm ci`, so the npm ci layer's cache key ends up depending on the entire source tree rather than on `package.json` alone.
Explains that because of this ordering, any source-code edit — even one unrelated to dependencies — invalidates the COPY layer and forces `npm ci` to reinstall from scratch on every build.
Prescribes the concrete fix: `COPY package*.json ./` then `RUN npm ci` (before copying the rest), followed by `COPY . .` last, so the npm ci layer's cache key depends only on the manifest checksum.

States the fix's effect precisely: a code-only change still invalidates `COPY . .` but leaves the preceding `npm ci` layer CACHED, and proposes verifying this by building twice with only a code file changed and checking the log shows `npm ci` as CACHED.

Runtime stage should be distroless: it ships no shell/coreutils (`/bin/sh`, `/bin/bash`, busybox), so `docker exec ... sh` fails immediately ("executable file not found") — satisfying the no-exec requirement while also denying an attacker post-exploitation tooling and cutting CVE surface versus a full-OS image like ubuntu.

Because bcrypt is a native module needing C++ compilation, use a multi-stage build: a `builder` stage carries the compile toolchain (gcc, make, python for node-gyp) to build the native addon, then only the finished `node_modules` and app code are copied (`COPY --from=builder`) into the distroless runtime stage — the toolchain itself never ships.

The specific pitfall: a compiled native module binary is linked against a particular libc family (musl vs glibc) at build time, so builder and runtime images must share the same libc family — since the distroless runtime is glibc-based, the builder must be `node:20-slim` or `node:20` (glibc), NOT `node:20-alpine` (musl), even though alpine is smaller.

If the libc families mismatch (e.g. an alpine/musl builder feeding a glibc distroless runtime), the compiled `bcrypt.node` binary fails to load at runtime, surfacing as an error like `libc.musl-*.so.1: cannot open shared object file` (or the reverse mismatch).

Distroless is not "0 CVE": frame it to security's manager as drastically cutting OS surface and removing the build toolchain, but residual CVEs remain from base OS libs (e.g. libssl3) and the app's own dependencies (node_modules, including transitive deps), so regular scanning (Trivy) and dependency bumps are still required alongside it.
